newsitem.title: GREECE: Protesting Greek farmers block rail line.
newsitem.headline: Protesting Greek farmers block rail line.

text.p: Greek farmers briefly blocked a main rail line on Thursday to press economic demands and vowed to cut highways next week despite government threats to arrest them if they carry out the protests.
Scores of farmers stood and sat on rail lines between the central towns of Larissa and Karditsa for two hours as about 150 riot police watched from a distance, eyewitnesses said.
The farmers called off their initial plan to block the tracks for the whole day, saying they wanted to avoid clashes with police.
"The fact that they left is a good sign," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told reporters.
Farmers blockaded highways for 25 days in December and vowed to repeat the crippling action despite warnings from the government that this time they would face arrest and prosecution.

The farmers suspended their protests during the Christmas and New Year holidays. They said they would repeat the blockades if their demands for lower taxes, cheaper fuel and bigger state subsidies were not met.
The latest demonstrations began with rallies in central and northern Greece.

The farmers plan to occupy road toll booths on Friday to prevent the state from collecting fees from drivers. They say that on February 4 they will use tractors to block six key highway junctions -- cutting Greece in half as they did in December.
But Prime Minister Costas Simitis has pledged to keep the roads clear this time.

"We will not allow a group of farmers to cross the line. If they do they will face state forces," Reppas said earlier this week. "It would be fortunate not to speak about bloodshed and not to have bloodshed, to have self-restraint."
Government officials said hundreds of riot police units were on standby near Karditsa and Larissa, headquarters of the farmers' protest.
Simitis has made minimal concessions to the farmers, saying his government cannot alter the European Union's agriculture policy or risk Greece's economic future to satisfy a single group.

The farmers are demanding lower fuel costs, cuts in value added tax on farm equipment, higher price supports -- especially for cotton -- and a $1.3 billion rescheduling of debts to the state Agricultural Bank.
